description: Matrices are nested lists (or SparseArray objects) and all the standard linear algebra operations work on them exactly for symbolic and rational input and numerically through LAPACK for machine numbers. This category covers products and solving, determinants and ranks, the eigen and matrix decompositions, matrix functions, vector geometry and the formatting and reshaping helpers.

tools.name: Dot
tools.description: The inner product operator, written infix as a period: it contracts the last index of its first argument with the first index of its second. It covers vector dot products, matrix-vector and matrix-matrix multiplication and general tensor contraction. For machine-number arrays it calls optimized BLAS routines and is the fastest way to multiply matrices.
tools.usage:
a . b
Dot[a, b, c]
matrix . vector
tools.notes: Dot is not the same as Times: a * b multiplies elementwise. For an outer product use Outer[Times, u, v] or KroneckerProduct.

tools.name: LinearSolve
tools.description: Solves the linear system m.x == b for x, using LU decomposition for square systems and least squares or minimum-norm solutions for rectangular ones. Called with one argument it returns a LinearSolveFunction that factors the matrix once and can then be applied to many right-hand sides efficiently. Sparse matrices are handled with sparse algorithms automatically.
tools.usage:
LinearSolve[m, b]
LinearSolve[m]
LinearSolve[m, b, Method -> "..."]
lsf = LinearSolve[m]; lsf[b]

parameters.name: Method
parameters.description: "LU", "Cholesky", "Krylov", "Multifrontal" or "Banded"; Krylov methods suit very large sparse systems.

parameters.name: Modulus
parameters.description: Solve over the integers modulo n.

tools.example:
LinearSolve[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, {5, 6}]
lsf = LinearSolve[{{2, 1}, {1, 3}}];
lsf[{1, 0}]
lsf[{0, 1}]
LinearSolve[SparseArray[{{i_, i_} -> 2, {i_, j_} /; Abs[i - j] == 1 -> -1}, {1000, 1000}], Range[1000]] // Short
tools.notes: Much faster and more stable than Inverse[m].b. For an over-determined system use LeastSquares, which is explicit about what it computes.

tools.name: Inverse
tools.description: Gives the inverse of a square matrix, exactly for symbolic and rational entries and numerically for machine numbers. It issues a message and returns unevaluated for singular matrices. Computing an inverse explicitly is rarely the best way to solve a system; use LinearSolve instead.
tools.usage:
Inverse[m]
Inverse[m, Modulus -> n]
Inverse[m, Method -> "CofactorExpansion"]
tools.notes: For numerically ill-conditioned matrices the explicit inverse loses accuracy; check with the condition number or use PseudoInverse.

tools.name: PseudoInverse
tools.description: Gives the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of a rectangular or singular matrix, computed from the singular value decomposition. Multiplying it by a right-hand side yields the least-squares solution of minimum norm. The Tolerance option controls which small singular values are treated as zero.
tools.usage:
PseudoInverse[m]
PseudoInverse[m, Tolerance -> t]
tools.example:
PseudoInverse[{{1, 2}, {2, 4}}]
PseudoInverse[{{1, 1}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}}]
PseudoInverse[a] . b
PseudoInverse[m, Tolerance -> 10^-8]
tools.notes: LeastSquares[m, b] is more efficient than PseudoInverse[m].b when only the solution vector is required.

tools.name: LeastSquares
tools.description: Finds the vector x minimizing Norm[m.x - b], i.e. the least-squares solution of an over-determined linear system. For rank-deficient systems it returns the minimum-norm solution. A Tikhonov regularization parameter can be supplied to stabilize ill-conditioned problems.
tools.usage:
LeastSquares[m, b]
LeastSquares[m, b, Tolerance -> t]
LeastSquares[m, b, "Tikhonov" -> lambda]
tools.example:
LeastSquares[{{1, 1}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}}, {1, 2, 4}]
LeastSquares[designMatrix, observations]
Norm[m . LeastSquares[m, b] - b]
tools.notes: This is the numerical core of linear regression; LinearModelFit wraps it with statistical diagnostics.

tools.name: Det
tools.description: Gives the determinant of a square matrix, computed exactly for symbolic and rational entries and by LU factorization for machine numbers. A zero determinant means the matrix is singular, though for floating-point matrices a small determinant is a poor conditioning test. The Modulus option computes the determinant over a finite field.
tools.usage:
Det[m]
Det[m, Modulus -> n]
Det[m, Method -> "CofactorExpansion"]
tools.example:
Det[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
Det[{{a, b}, {c, d}}]
Det[IdentityMatrix[5]]
Solve[Det[m - lambda IdentityMatrix[2]] == 0, lambda]
tools.notes: Use MatrixRank or SingularValueList rather than Det to test numerical singularity, since determinants scale badly with dimension.

tools.name: Tr
tools.description: Gives the trace of a matrix, the sum of its diagonal elements, and more generally contracts the main diagonal of a tensor. A second argument replaces Plus with another combining function, so Tr[m, Times] gives the product of the diagonal. Tr[m] equals the sum of the eigenvalues, which makes it useful for checking eigenvalue computations.
tools.usage:
Tr[m]
Tr[m, f]
Tr[tensor, f, n]
tools.example:
Tr[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
Tr[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, Times]
Tr[m] == Total[Eigenvalues[m]]
Tr[IdentityMatrix[4]]
tools.notes: Do not confuse Tr with Transpose or with Diagonal, which returns the diagonal elements as a list without summing them.

tools.name: ConjugateTranspose
tools.description: Gives the Hermitian adjoint of a matrix: the transpose with every entry complex-conjugated. It is the correct transpose for complex matrices in inner-product computations and the operation used to test for Hermitian matrices. For real matrices it coincides with Transpose.
tools.usage:
ConjugateTranspose[m]
ConjugateTranspose[m, perm]
tools.example:
ConjugateTranspose[{{1, I}, {2, 3}}]
ConjugateTranspose[m] . m
HermitianMatrixQ[m]
ConjugateTranspose[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]

tools.name: Eigenvalues
tools.description: Gives the eigenvalues of a square matrix, exactly for small symbolic matrices and numerically via LAPACK for machine numbers. Eigenvalues[m, k] gives the k largest-magnitude eigenvalues, and Eigenvalues[m, -k] the k smallest, which is the efficient path for large sparse matrices. Eigenvalues[{m, a}] solves the generalized problem m.v == lambda a.v.
tools.usage:
Eigenvalues[m]
Eigenvalues[m, k]
Eigenvalues[m, -k]
Eigenvalues[{m, a}]
Eigenvalues[N[m]]
tools.example:
Eigenvalues[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
Eigenvalues[{{2, 0}, {0, 3}}]
Eigenvalues[N[RandomReal[1, {200, 200}]], 5]
Eigenvalues[{{a, b}, {b, a}}]
Eigenvalues[{m, IdentityMatrix[3]}]
tools.notes: Eigenvalues are returned in order of decreasing absolute value for numeric matrices; symbolic results for matrices of size 5 or more usually involve Root objects.

tools.name: Eigenvectors
tools.description: Gives the eigenvectors of a square matrix as a list of row vectors, in the same order as the corresponding eigenvalues. Degenerate or defective matrices produce zero vectors to pad the result to full length. As with Eigenvalues, a count argument requests only the largest or smallest few, which is essential for large sparse problems.
tools.usage:
Eigenvectors[m]
Eigenvectors[m, k]
Eigenvectors[{m, a}]
tools.example:
Eigenvectors[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
Eigenvectors[{{2, 0}, {0, 3}}]
Eigenvectors[N[m], 3]
Normalize /@ Eigenvectors[symmetricMatrix]
tools.notes: Eigenvectors are rows of the returned matrix, so Transpose[Eigenvectors[m]] is the matrix whose columns diagonalize m. They are not normalized unless the matrix is numeric.

tools.name: Eigensystem
tools.description: Returns {eigenvalues, eigenvectors} together in a single computation, which is faster and guarantees the pairing is consistent. It accepts the same count and generalized-problem arguments as Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors. Use it whenever both parts are needed.
tools.usage:
Eigensystem[m]
Eigensystem[m, k]
Eigensystem[{m, a}]
tools.example:
{vals, vecs} = Eigensystem[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}];
vals
vecs
Eigensystem[N[m], 3]
Eigensystem[{{0, 1}, {-1, 0}}]

tools.name: CharacteristicPolynomial
tools.description: Gives the characteristic polynomial Det[m - x IdentityMatrix] of a square matrix as an explicit polynomial in the given variable. Its roots are the eigenvalues, and its coefficients are the invariants of the matrix. A generalized form CharacteristicPolynomial[{m, a}, x] handles the pencil m - x a.
tools.usage:
CharacteristicPolynomial[m, x]
CharacteristicPolynomial[{m, a}, x]
CharacteristicPolynomial[m, x, Modulus -> p]
tools.example:
CharacteristicPolynomial[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, x]
Solve[CharacteristicPolynomial[m, x] == 0, x]
CharacteristicPolynomial[{{a, b}, {c, d}}, lambda]
Factor[CharacteristicPolynomial[{{2, 0}, {0, 2}}, x]]
tools.notes: MinimalPolynomial gives the lowest-degree annihilating polynomial, which divides the characteristic polynomial and detects repeated structure.

tools.name: SingularValueDecomposition
tools.description: Factors a matrix as m == u . sigma . ConjugateTranspose[v], where u and v have orthonormal columns and sigma is diagonal with non-negative entries. The SVD is the most numerically stable decomposition and underlies rank determination, pseudoinverses, least squares and principal component analysis. A rank argument computes only the leading singular triplets.
tools.usage:
SingularValueDecomposition[m]
SingularValueDecomposition[m, k]
SingularValueDecomposition[m, Tolerance -> t]
tools.example:
{u, s, v} = SingularValueDecomposition[N[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}, {5, 6}}]];
u . s . ConjugateTranspose[v]
Diagonal[s]
SingularValueDecomposition[N[m], 2]
tools.notes: SingularValueList returns just the singular values, which is faster when the vectors are not needed; their ratio is the condition number.

tools.name: SingularValueList
tools.description: Gives the non-zero singular values of a matrix in decreasing order, without computing the singular vectors. The count of values above a tolerance is the numerical rank, and the ratio of largest to smallest is the 2-norm condition number. A count argument returns only the largest few.
tools.usage:
SingularValueList[m]
SingularValueList[m, k]
SingularValueList[m, Tolerance -> t]
tools.example:
SingularValueList[N[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]]
First[SingularValueList[m]]/Last[SingularValueList[m]]
Length[SingularValueList[m]]
SingularValueList[N[m], 3]

tools.name: LUDecomposition
tools.description: Computes the LU decomposition with partial pivoting, returning {lu, permutation, conditionNumber} where the combined lu matrix holds both triangular factors. LUBackSubstitution then solves systems with the factored matrix. It is the factorization underlying LinearSolve and Det for general square matrices.
tools.usage:
LUDecomposition[m]
{lu, p, c} = LUDecomposition[m]
LUBackSubstitution[{lu, p, c}, b]
tools.example:
{lu, p, c} = LUDecomposition[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}];
lu
p
LUBackSubstitution[{lu, p, c}, {5, 6}]
tools.notes: The third element estimates the reciprocal condition number; a very small value warns that the solution will be inaccurate.

tools.name: QRDecomposition
tools.description: Factors a matrix as m == ConjugateTranspose[q] . r with q having orthonormal rows and r upper triangular. It is the stable way to solve least-squares problems and to orthogonalize a set of vectors. The Pivoting option adds column pivoting for rank-deficient matrices.
tools.usage:
QRDecomposition[m]
QRDecomposition[m, Pivoting -> True]
tools.example:
{q, r} = QRDecomposition[N[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}, {5, 6}}]];
ConjugateTranspose[q] . r
q . ConjugateTranspose[q]
QRDecomposition[m, Pivoting -> True]
tools.notes: Note the convention: q is returned so that m == ConjugateTranspose[q].r, i.e. the rows of q are the orthonormal basis vectors.

tools.name: CholeskyDecomposition
tools.description: Factors a Hermitian positive-definite matrix as ConjugateTranspose[u] . u with u upper triangular. It is about twice as fast as LU for such matrices and is the standard step for sampling multivariate normals and solving normal equations. It fails with a message if the matrix is not positive definite, which makes it a practical positive-definiteness test.
tools.usage: CholeskyDecomposition[m]
tools.example:
u = CholeskyDecomposition[{{4, 2}, {2, 3}}];
ConjugateTranspose[u] . u
CholeskyDecomposition[N[covarianceMatrix]]
PositiveDefiniteMatrixQ[m]

tools.name: SchurDecomposition
tools.description: Gives {q, t} with q unitary and t upper triangular (or quasi-triangular in the real case) such that m == q . t . ConjugateTranspose[q]. The diagonal of t holds the eigenvalues, and the decomposition always exists even for defective matrices where diagonalization fails. RealBlockDiagonalForm controls whether complex eigenvalues appear as 2x2 real blocks.
tools.usage:
SchurDecomposition[m]
SchurDecomposition[m, RealBlockDiagonalForm -> False]
SchurDecomposition[{m, a}]
tools.example:
{q, t} = SchurDecomposition[N[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]];
q . t . ConjugateTranspose[q]
Diagonal[t]
SchurDecomposition[N[m], RealBlockDiagonalForm -> False]
tools.notes: The Schur form is the numerically reliable route to matrix functions and eigenvalues of non-symmetric matrices, which is why MatrixFunction uses it.

tools.name: JordanDecomposition
tools.description: Gives {s, j} such that m == s . j . Inverse[s] with j in Jordan canonical form, revealing the eigenvalue structure including defective blocks. It is an exact symbolic computation and is numerically unstable, so it should be used on exact rational or symbolic matrices only. The Jordan form shows geometric versus algebraic multiplicity directly.
tools.usage: JordanDecomposition[m]
tools.example:
{s, j} = JordanDecomposition[{{1, 1}, {0, 1}}];
j
s . j . Inverse[s]
JordanDecomposition[{{2, 1, 0}, {0, 2, 0}, {0, 0, 3}}]
tools.notes: Never apply JordanDecomposition to floating-point matrices; use SchurDecomposition instead for numerical work.

tools.name: MatrixExp
tools.description: Computes the matrix exponential, the sum of the power series m^k/k!, which is not the elementwise exponential. MatrixExp[m, v] computes the product MatrixExp[m].v more efficiently than forming the matrix first. It is the solution operator of the linear system y'[t] == m.y[t] and appears throughout control theory and dynamics.
tools.usage:
MatrixExp[m]
MatrixExp[m, v]
MatrixExp[m t]
tools.example:
MatrixExp[{{0, 1}, {-1, 0}}]
MatrixExp[{{0, 1}, {0, 0}}]
MatrixExp[N[m], v]
MatrixExp[a t] . y0
tools.notes: Exp[m] applies the scalar exponential elementwise and is a completely different operation; MatrixExp is the true matrix function.

tools.name: MatrixPower
tools.description: Raises a square matrix to an integer, negative or symbolic power using repeated squaring or eigendecomposition. Negative powers require the matrix to be invertible. MatrixPower[m, n, v] applies the power to a vector without forming the intermediate matrix, which is efficient for large sparse matrices.
tools.usage:
MatrixPower[m, n]
MatrixPower[m, n, v]
MatrixPower[m, -1]
tools.example:
MatrixPower[{{1, 1}, {1, 0}}, 10]
MatrixPower[{{2, 0}, {0, 3}}, -1]
MatrixPower[m, 100, v]
MatrixPower[{{1, 1}, {0, 1}}, n]
tools.notes: m^n with ordinary Power raises each element to the n-th power; use MatrixPower for the matrix product meaning.

tools.name: MatrixFunction
tools.description: Applies a general scalar function to a matrix in the matrix-function sense, defined through the eigen- or Schur decomposition rather than elementwise. MatrixFunction[Sin, m] gives the matrix sine, MatrixFunction[Sqrt, m] a matrix square root. It handles defective matrices correctly using the Jordan or Schur-Parlett approach.
tools.usage:
MatrixFunction[f, m]
MatrixFunction[f, m, v]
tools.example:
MatrixFunction[Exp, {{0, 1}, {-1, 0}}]
MatrixFunction[Sqrt, {{4, 0}, {0, 9}}]
MatrixFunction[Log, N[m]]
MatrixFunction[#^2 &, m]
tools.notes: MatrixExp and MatrixPower are optimized special cases. The function must be analytic on the spectrum of the matrix for the result to be well defined.

tools.name: MatrixRank
tools.description: Gives the rank of a matrix, i.e. the number of linearly independent rows or columns. It is computed exactly for symbolic and rational matrices and from the singular values with a tolerance for machine numbers. Comparing the rank to the dimensions tells you whether a linear system is consistent and whether the solution is unique.
tools.usage:
MatrixRank[m]
MatrixRank[m, Tolerance -> t]
MatrixRank[m, Modulus -> p]
tools.example:
MatrixRank[{{1, 2}, {2, 4}}]
MatrixRank[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
MatrixRank[N[m], Tolerance -> 10^-8]
MatrixRank[{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}, {7, 8, 9}}]
tools.notes: For floating-point matrices the answer depends on the tolerance; inspect SingularValueList to see whether there is a clear rank gap.

tools.name: NullSpace
tools.description: Gives a list of basis vectors for the null space (kernel) of a matrix, i.e. the solutions of m.x == 0. An empty result means the matrix has full column rank. Together with a particular solution from LinearSolve it describes the complete solution set of an under-determined system.
tools.usage:
NullSpace[m]
NullSpace[m, Tolerance -> t]
NullSpace[m, Modulus -> p]
tools.example:
NullSpace[{{1, 2}, {2, 4}}]
NullSpace[{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}}]
NullSpace[{{1, 0}, {0, 1}}]
m . First[NullSpace[m]]
tools.notes: The basis returned is not orthonormal; apply Orthogonalize if an orthonormal basis is required.

tools.name: RowReduce
tools.description: Puts a matrix into reduced row echelon form by Gaussian elimination with pivoting. Applied to an augmented matrix it solves a linear system by hand-style elimination and exposes which variables are free. It works exactly for symbolic and rational entries and numerically with a tolerance for machine numbers.
tools.usage:
RowReduce[m]
RowReduce[m, Modulus -> p]
RowReduce[m, ZeroTest -> f]
tools.example:
RowReduce[{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}}]
RowReduce[{{1, 2, 5}, {3, 4, 6}}]
RowReduce[IdentityMatrix[3]]
RowReduce[{{1, 2}, {2, 4}}]
tools.notes: Symbolic matrices may need a ZeroTest that calls Simplify, otherwise entries that are zero only after simplification are used as pivots.

tools.name: IdentityMatrix
tools.description: Gives the n x n identity matrix, or a rectangular matrix with ones on the main diagonal when given a dimension pair. SparseArray -> Automatic produces a sparse identity, which is essential for large dimensions. It is the starting point for building many structured matrices.
tools.usage:
IdentityMatrix[n]
IdentityMatrix[{m, n}]
IdentityMatrix[n, SparseArray]
tools.example:
IdentityMatrix[3]
IdentityMatrix[{2, 3}]
m - lambda IdentityMatrix[Length[m]]
IdentityMatrix[10000, SparseArray]

tools.name: DiagonalMatrix
tools.description: Builds a matrix with the given list on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. A second argument k places the list on the k-th super- or sub-diagonal, which is how tridiagonal and banded matrices are assembled. A dimension argument makes the result rectangular or larger than the list.
tools.usage:
DiagonalMatrix[list]
DiagonalMatrix[list, k]
DiagonalMatrix[list, k, n]
DiagonalMatrix[SparseArray[list]]
tools.example:
DiagonalMatrix[{1, 2, 3}]
DiagonalMatrix[{1, 1}, 1]
DiagonalMatrix[{1, 1}, -1] + DiagonalMatrix[{2, 2, 2}]
DiagonalMatrix[Range[1000], 0, 1000]
tools.notes: For large banded matrices SparseArray with Band is far more memory-efficient than building a dense DiagonalMatrix.

tools.name: Diagonal
tools.description: Extracts the main diagonal of a matrix as a list, or the k-th diagonal when a second argument is given. It is the inverse of DiagonalMatrix and is used to read the eigenvalues off a triangular or Schur form. For non-square matrices it takes the diagonal that exists.
tools.usage:
Diagonal[m]
Diagonal[m, k]
tools.example:
Diagonal[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
Diagonal[{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}, {7, 8, 9}}, 1]
Total[Diagonal[m]] == Tr[m]
Diagonal[schurT]

tools.name: KroneckerProduct
tools.description: Forms the Kronecker (tensor) product of matrices, producing a block matrix in which each element of the first is multiplied by the whole second matrix. It is the standard construction for composite quantum systems, two-dimensional finite-difference operators and separable transforms. It accepts any number of arguments and works on vectors and higher tensors as well.
tools.usage: KroneckerProduct[m1, m2, ...]
tools.example:
KroneckerProduct[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, IdentityMatrix[2]]
KroneckerProduct[PauliMatrix[1], PauliMatrix[3]]
Dimensions[KroneckerProduct[RandomReal[1, {3, 3}], RandomReal[1, {4, 4}]]]
KroneckerProduct[{1, 2}, {3, 4}]
tools.notes: Outer[Times, a, b] gives the same numbers but keeps the four-index tensor structure rather than flattening into a block matrix.

tools.name: Cross
tools.description: Gives the cross product of two three-dimensional vectors, written infix with the \[Cross] operator. More generally Cross of n-1 vectors in n dimensions gives a vector orthogonal to all of them. The result is perpendicular to both inputs with magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram they span.
tools.usage:
Cross[a, b]
a \[Cross] b
Cross[v1, v2, ..., vn-1]
tools.example:
Cross[{1, 0, 0}, {0, 1, 0}]
Cross[{a1, a2, a3}, {b1, b2, b3}]
Norm[Cross[u, v]]
Cross[{1, 2}]
tools.notes: Cross[v] with a single 2D vector gives the perpendicular vector {-v2, v1}, which is often useful in plane geometry.

tools.name: Norm
tools.description: Gives the norm of a vector or matrix. For vectors the default is the Euclidean 2-norm and the second argument selects any p-norm or Infinity for the maximum absolute value. For matrices Norm gives the induced operator norm, with "Frobenius" available as a named option.
tools.usage:
Norm[v]
Norm[v, p]
Norm[v, Infinity]
Norm[m, "Frobenius"]
tools.example:
Norm[{3, 4}]
Norm[{1, -2, 3}, 1]
Norm[{1, -2, 3}, Infinity]
Norm[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, "Frobenius"]
Norm[a - b]
tools.notes: The matrix 2-norm is the largest singular value and is comparatively expensive; the Frobenius norm is much cheaper when an exact operator norm is not needed.

tools.name: Normalize
tools.description: Scales a vector to unit length, or scales any expression by a supplied norm function. Normalize[v, f] divides by f[v], which allows normalization by the 1-norm, the maximum, or a probability sum. The zero vector is returned unchanged rather than causing a division by zero.
tools.usage:
Normalize[v]
Normalize[v, f]
tools.example:
Normalize[{3, 4}]
Normalize[{1, 1, 1}]
Normalize[{1, 2, 3}, Total]
Normalize[psi, Norm]

tools.name: Projection
tools.description: Gives the orthogonal projection of one vector onto another, or onto a subspace with respect to a specified inner product function. It is the building block of the Gram-Schmidt process and of least-squares geometry. A third argument supplies a custom inner product, so it also works for function spaces.
tools.usage:
Projection[u, v]
Projection[u, v, f]
tools.example:
Projection[{1, 2}, {1, 0}]
Projection[{5, 5}, {1, 1}]
u - Projection[u, v]
Projection[f, g, Integrate[#1 #2, {x, 0, 1}] &]

tools.name: Orthogonalize
tools.description: Produces an orthonormal basis from a list of vectors using Gram-Schmidt by default, or Householder, QR or SVD-based methods. Linearly dependent inputs yield zero vectors in the corresponding positions. A custom inner product function makes it work for polynomials and other function spaces, which is how classical orthogonal polynomial families can be generated.
tools.usage:
Orthogonalize[{v1, v2, ...}]
Orthogonalize[vectors, f]
Orthogonalize[vectors, Method -> "Householder"]
tools.example:
Orthogonalize[{{1, 1}, {1, 0}}]
Orthogonalize[{{3, 0}, {1, 2}, {0, 5}}]
Orthogonalize[{1, x, x^2}, Integrate[#1 #2, {x, -1, 1}] &]
Orthogonalize[N[vectors], Method -> "Householder"]

tools.name: VectorAngle
tools.description: Gives the angle in radians between two vectors, computed stably from their inner product and norms. It works in any dimension and for complex vectors. Use it for geometric computations and for measuring similarity between feature vectors.
tools.usage: VectorAngle[u, v]
tools.example:
VectorAngle[{1, 0}, {0, 1}]
VectorAngle[{1, 1}, {1, 0}]
VectorAngle[{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}] // N
Cos[VectorAngle[u, v]]
tools.notes: Cos[VectorAngle[u, v]] is the cosine similarity used in information retrieval; CosineDistance computes 1 minus that directly.

tools.name: MatrixForm
tools.description: Displays a nested list in traditional two-dimensional matrix layout with brackets. It is a formatting wrapper only: the result is not a matrix for computation, so never assign MatrixForm output to a variable used in arithmetic. Use it as a postfix // MatrixForm at the end of an expression.
tools.usage:
MatrixForm[m]
m // MatrixForm
TableForm[m]
tools.example:
MatrixForm[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
Inverse[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}] // MatrixForm
TableForm[data, TableHeadings -> {rows, cols}]
Grid[m, Frame -> All]
tools.notes: A very common mistake is m = MatrixForm[...]; subsequent Dot or Inverse calls then fail. Keep the raw list and format only at display time.

tools.name: ArrayFlatten
tools.description: Assembles a matrix of matrices into a single flat matrix, the standard way to build block matrices. Scalar 0 entries are expanded into zero blocks of the right size automatically. A level argument generalizes the operation to higher-rank block tensors.
tools.usage:
ArrayFlatten[blocks]
ArrayFlatten[blocks, r]
tools.example:
ArrayFlatten[{{IdentityMatrix[2], 0}, {0, {{5}}}}]
ArrayFlatten[{{a, b}, {c, d}}]
ArrayFlatten[{{m, ConstantArray[0, {2, 2}]}, {ConstantArray[0, {2, 2}], m}}]
tools.notes: Flatten[blocks, {{1, 3}, {2, 4}}] does the same thing when every block has identical dimensions.

tools.name: ArrayReshape
tools.description: Rearranges the elements of an array into a new shape, padding with zeros or a supplied filler if the new shape needs more elements and truncating if it needs fewer. It is the fast way to convert a flat list into a matrix or tensor. Unlike Partition it never leaves a ragged remainder.
tools.usage:
ArrayReshape[list, dims]
ArrayReshape[list, dims, padding]
tools.example:
ArrayReshape[Range[6], {2, 3}]
ArrayReshape[Range[4], {3, 3}]
ArrayReshape[Range[4], {3, 3}, x]
ArrayReshape[Flatten[m], Reverse[Dimensions[m]]]

tools.name: MatrixQ
tools.description: Tests whether an expression is a rectangular two-dimensional array, optionally requiring every element to satisfy a test such as NumericQ. VectorQ and ArrayQ are the corresponding tests for one-dimensional and general arrays. These are the standard argument guards for functions expecting matrix input.
tools.usage:
MatrixQ[expr]
MatrixQ[expr, test]
VectorQ[expr, test]
ArrayQ[expr, depth, test]
tools.example:
MatrixQ[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
MatrixQ[{{1, 2}, {3}}]
MatrixQ[m, NumericQ]
